lessonTitle: Upper Gastrointestinal Disease: Dyspepsia, Bleeding and Helicobacter pylori

blocks.text: A 61-year-old builder has taken diclofenac for back pain for two months. This morning he vomits a cupful of coffee-ground material, passes a tarry black stool and feels faint on standing. Minutes matter: his pulse is 118 and his blood pressure is 92/54. Upper gastrointestinal disease ranges from the annoyance of dyspepsia to life-threatening bleeding, and the skill is knowing which patient is which.

blocks.markdown: The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid from parietal cells and mucus and bicarbonate protect the mucosa. **Dyspepsia** is upper abdominal pain or discomfort, bloating, early satiety or nausea, usually related to meals. Most dyspepsia is benign (functional dyspepsia, gastro-oesophageal reflux, peptic ulcer disease), but a minority is caused by cancer, so the management of dyspepsia is organised around **alarm features**. The two commonest causes of peptic ulcers are *Helicobacter pylori* infection and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and the production of protective prostaglandins.

blocks.title: Alarm features that mandate endoscopy
blocks.text: Dysphagia (progressive difficulty swallowing), unintentional weight loss, persistent vomiting, iron-deficiency anaemia, upper gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis or melaena), an epigastric mass, and new-onset dyspepsia in an older patient (UK guidance uses age 55 and over with other symptoms such as weight loss) all need urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Younger patients without alarm features are managed with lifestyle advice, review of NSAIDs, a trial of proton pump inhibitor, or testing for H. pylori and eradication if positive.

rows: Epigastric pain, NSAID or aspirin use, H. pylori; melaena
Commonest cause; erosion of an artery; endoscopic therapy
Known cirrhosis or portal hypertension, massive haematemesis
Terlipressin, antibiotics and band ligation; high mortality
Forceful retching or vomiting, then bright red blood
Mucosal tear at the oesophagogastric junction; usually self-limiting
blocks.caption: Causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

blocks.markdown: **Resuscitation in upper GI bleeding.** Assess airway, breathing and circulation first. Give oxygen if needed, insert two large-bore intravenous cannulae, send blood for full blood count, urea, group and crossmatch, and clotting, and start fluid resuscitation, using blood early in major haemorrhage. For stable patients a restrictive transfusion policy is used (transfuse when haemoglobin falls below about 70 g/L, aiming for 70 to 80 g/L), because over-transfusion can raise portal pressure and rebleeding in variceal bleeding. Risk is stratified using the **Glasgow-Blatchford score**, which uses urea, haemoglobin, systolic blood pressure, pulse, melaena, syncope, liver disease and heart failure to identify low-risk patients who can be managed as outpatients. Upper GI endoscopy is performed after resuscitation, within 24 hours (sooner if unstable), to diagnose and treat the lesion (clips, thermal therapy or adrenaline injection for ulcers; banding for varices). Stop NSAIDs and anticoagulants as appropriate.

blocks.caption: A simple bedside marker; values above about 1.0 suggest significant haemodynamic compromise (normal about 0.5 to 0.7).

blocks.title: Shock index at the bedside
blocks.prompt: A patient with melaena has heart rate 108 beats/min and systolic blood pressure 100 mmHg. Calculate the shock index and interpret it.

steps.text: Divide heart rate by systolic blood pressure.
A value above 1.0 signals haemodynamic compromise and significant blood loss, even though the blood pressure alone appears acceptable.
Treat as significant bleeding: large-bore access, fluid or blood, urgent bloods, and early endoscopy.

blocks.answer: Shock index 1.08: significant bleeding likely; resuscitate and arrange early endoscopy.

blocks.caption: Estimated adult blood volume is about 70 mL/kg.

blocks.title: How much blood has been lost?
blocks.prompt: An 80 kg man is estimated to have lost 15% of his blood volume. Calculate the volume lost.

steps.text: About 15% loss is often compensated by tachycardia and vasoconstriction with a near-normal blood pressure; losses of 30% or more cause hypotension and shock.

blocks.markdown: **Helicobacter pylori.** *H. pylori* is a spiral Gram-negative bacterium that colonises the gastric mucosa, producing urease that makes ammonia and buffers acid. It causes chronic gastritis and is a major cause of duodenal and gastric ulcers; it is also a risk factor for gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. **Testing:** non-invasive tests that detect active infection are the 13C-urea breath test and the stool antigen test. Because proton pump inhibitors and antibiotics suppress the organism, they cause false-negative results: stop PPIs for 2 weeks and antibiotics for 4 weeks before testing. Serology shows exposure, not current infection, and is not used to confirm cure. **Eradication:** triple therapy of a PPI with two antibiotics (commonly amoxicillin with clarithromycin or metronidazole, chosen using local resistance data and allergy history) for 7 days is standard in UK guidance. Test of cure (breath or stool antigen at least 4 weeks after treatment) is indicated after a gastric ulcer, complicated ulcer or MALT lymphoma, and for persistent symptoms. Gastric ulcers should have biopsies taken and healing documented, because they can be malignant.

items: Duodenal ulcer pain tends to be epigastric, often at night and may be relieved by food; gastric ulcer pain often worsens with eating and may be accompanied by weight loss.
Complications of peptic ulcer include bleeding, perforation (sudden severe abdominal pain with free air under the diaphragm) and gastric outlet obstruction.
Review and stop NSAIDs where possible; give a PPI if they must continue.
Post-endoscopy: PPI for healing; eradicate H. pylori if positive.
Reflux: alginate or PPI, lifestyle changes, endoscopy if alarm features or persistent symptoms (Barrett oesophagus risk).

points: Alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, anaemia, bleeding, mass, older age with new dyspepsia) mandate urgent endoscopy.
The commonest cause of upper GI bleeding is peptic ulceration, from H. pylori or NSAIDs; varices, Mallory-Weiss tears and malignancy are other causes.
Resuscitate first (ABC, IV access, fluid or blood, restrictive transfusion), then risk stratify with the Glasgow-Blatchford score and endoscope within 24 hours.
Test for H. pylori with a breath or stool antigen test off PPIs and antibiotics, eradicate with a PPI and two antibiotics, and confirm cure where indicated.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has 3 months of epigastric discomfort and progressive difficulty swallowing solid food. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks first
Test and treat for H. pylori alone

distractorRationale.a: Correct: dysphagia is an alarm feature requiring urgent endoscopy.
distractorRationale.b: A PPI trial would delay diagnosis of possible malignancy.
distractorRationale.c: Test-and-treat is for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features.
distractorRationale.d: Reassurance is inappropriate with alarm symptoms.

questions.explanation: Progressive dysphagia suggests an oesophageal or gastric lesion, including cancer, which must be excluded endoscopically. Empirical acid suppression can mask or delay recognition.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an alarm feature in a patient presenting with dyspepsia?

options.text: Symptoms for two weeks after a spicy meal

distractorRationale.a: Correct: weight loss suggests possible malignancy.
distractorRationale.b: Postprandial bloating is common in functional dyspepsia.
distractorRationale.c: Responsiveness to antacids is reassuring, not alarming.
distractorRationale.d: Short-lived symptoms after a trigger are benign.

questions.explanation: Unintentional weight loss, along with dysphagia, persistent vomiting, anaemia, GI bleeding and an epigastric mass, are the alarm features that prompt urgent endoscopy. The other options are common in benign dyspepsia.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman taking low-dose aspirin and prednisolone vomits a large volume of fresh red blood. She is pale with cold peripheries, heart rate 126 beats/min and blood pressure 84/48 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Resuscitation with two large-bore cannulae, fluids or blood and urgent bloods, followed by endoscopy
Start a PPI tablet and observe at home

questions.correctOptionText: Resuscitation with two large-bore cannulae, fluids or blood and urgent bloods, followed by endoscopy

distractorRationale.a: Correct: haemodynamic compromise requires resuscitation first.
distractorRationale.c: Iron does not treat acute bleeding.
distractorRationale.d: Observation at home is inappropriate in a shocked patient.

questions.explanation: Tachycardia with hypotension and cold peripheries shows major blood loss, so airway, breathing and circulation are addressed first with intravenous access and volume or blood replacement. Endoscopy follows resuscitation, and aspirin is reviewed once the bleeding is controlled.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old has several episodes of forceful vomiting after drinking heavily, followed by a small volume of bright red haematemesis. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: retching followed by bleeding indicates a mucosal tear.
distractorRationale.b: Varices need portal hypertension, usually with massive bleeding.
distractorRationale.c: Ulcers would have a pain history and NSAID or H. pylori context.
distractorRationale.d: Cancer would be unlikely in a young man without alarm features.

questions.explanation: A tear at the oesophagogastric junction results from a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure during retching. It is usually small and self-limiting, though it is confirmed at endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man taking omeprazole 20 mg daily is to be tested for H. pylori with a urea breath test. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Stop the PPI for 2 weeks before testing, if clinically safe
Continue the PPI because it improves test accuracy
Take antibiotics for a week before the test
Test with serology instead as PPIs do not affect it

questions.correctOptionText: Stop the PPI for 2 weeks before testing, if clinically safe

distractorRationale.a: Correct: PPIs reduce bacterial load and cause false-negative breath tests.
distractorRationale.b: PPIs reduce accuracy, not improve it.
distractorRationale.d: Serology cannot confirm current infection or cure, so it is not preferred for this indication.

questions.explanation: PPIs suppress H. pylori and urease activity, so breath and stool antigen tests can be falsely negative. They should be stopped for 2 weeks and antibiotics for 4 weeks before testing where it is safe to do so.

questions.stem: A patient with haematemesis has heart rate 124 beats/min and systolic blood pressure 88 mmHg. Calculate the shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Shock index = 124 / 88 = 1.41. A value above 1.0 indicates significant haemodynamic compromise, so this patient needs urgent resuscitation and early endoscopy.

questions.stem: A 65 kg patient with a variceal bleed has lost approximately 30% of the blood volume. Taking blood volume as 70 mL/kg, calculate the volume lost in mL.
questions.explanation: Blood volume is 70 x 65 = 4550 mL, and 30% of this is 1365 mL. A loss of this magnitude causes hypotension and shock, so blood products and urgent haemostasis are needed.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with haematemesis and melaena. List the main causes of upper gastrointestinal bleeding and describe the initial resuscitation and the principles of subsequent management.
markingGuide: Causes: peptic ulcer, varices, Mallory-Weiss tear, erosive gastritis or oesophagitis, malignancy
Two large-bore cannulae; bloods including FBC, urea, group and crossmatch, clotting
Fluid and blood resuscitation, restrictive transfusion threshold (about 70 g/L)
Endoscopy within 24 hours or sooner if unstable, with endoscopic therapy
Stop NSAIDs; PPI after endoscopy; eradicate H. pylori
Varices: terlipressin, antibiotics and band ligation
questions.explanation: Resuscitation takes priority over diagnosis because haemorrhagic shock kills. Endoscopy then identifies the source and allows treatment, and further management addresses the cause, for example NSAID cessation and H. pylori eradication.

questions.stem: Explain how Helicobacter pylori infection is tested for and eradicated, and when a test of cure is needed.
markingGuide: Non-invasive tests: urea breath test and stool antigen test detect active infection
PPIs stopped 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks before testing to avoid false negatives
Serology shows exposure and is not used for cure
Eradication: PPI plus two antibiotics (for example amoxicillin with clarithromycin or metronidazole) for 7 days
Choice guided by allergy and local resistance
Test of cure at least 4 weeks after treatment for gastric ulcer, complicated ulcer, MALT lymphoma or persistent symptoms
Link to ulcer, gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma
questions.explanation: Tests rely on detecting live bacteria, so acid suppression or antibiotics cause false negatives. Eradication cures ulcer disease and reduces recurrence, and a test of cure is needed where failure to eradicate would be clinically important.

questions.stem: True or false: an IgG serology test is a suitable way to confirm that H. pylori has been eradicated 6 weeks after treatment.
questions.explanation: Antibodies remain positive long after the bacteria are gone, so serology cannot show cure. A urea breath test or stool antigen test, performed at least 4 weeks after treatment and off PPIs, should be used.
